=== ahmed2026secvuleval
- Research design: benchmark construction from NVD + GitHub commits, followed by an empirical evaluation of 5 LLMs inside a multi-agent pipeline, with manual judging of statement-level outputs (p. 4-p. 8).
- Data source(s): NVD CVEs (non-REJECTED) for products previously identified as C/C++ in BigVul, CVEFixes and PrimeVul, plus NVD keyword search ("C++", "C language", ".cpp"); only CVEs with an NVD "Patch" reference to a commit in the original (non-forked) repository; commit data via GitHub REST API (p. 4).
- Data availability: dataset on HuggingFace (arag0rn/SecVulEval) and code on GitHub (basimbd/SecVulEval) (p. 3); "friendly license" for research and commercial use (p. 12).
- Code availability: GitHub repository (p. 3).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): one-sided Mann-Whitney U tests compare the function length of detected vs. missed vulnerable functions (p. 12, p. 13). The detection metrics have no confidence intervals or significance tests, and repeated runs are not reported.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): only one run per model is reported, with no confidence intervals or tests on Table 3. The Mann-Whitney tests run across five models without multiple-comparison correction, but all p < 0.017, so they are likely robust (p. 13).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): the dataset, code and full prompts are released (p. 3, p. 14-p. 16), and hardware and temperature are reported (p. 8, p. 17). Whether the manual judgements for the 300 samples are released is not stated.
- Suggested by us [I]: run SAST tools (e.g. CodeQL, Cppcheck) and fine-tuned DL detectors on the same 300-sample subset; report statement-level recall under the stated definition with confidence intervals; compare the multi-agent pipeline against a single prompt, with and without context; split by CVE date to check for contamination.
=== chakraborty2024revisiting
- Data availability (public? link?): [A] Real-Vul and scripts released at https://zenodo.org/record/8206635 (p. 2).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V] Mann-Whitney U tests for cyclomatic complexity (TP vs FP p = 0.043; TN vs FN p = 0.014) and for LIME positive-token ratio in FP vs TP (p = 0.13, α = 0.05) (p. 10). No CIs or tests for the main performance comparisons.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No CIs or repeated runs for performance; Mann-Whitney tests only in side analyses, no multiple-comparison correction.
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [A] Dataset and scripts on Zenodo (p. 2); [I] augmentation strategies and LLM fine-tuning settings only in an online appendix / not reported.
=== ding2025vulnerability
- Data availability (public? link?): [A] Artifact released at https://github.com/DLVulDet/PrimeVul (p. 3).
- Code availability: [A] https://github.com/DLVulDet/PrimeVul (p. 3).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): not reported (number of runs / seeds not reported; results are point estimates).
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No seeds, repeated runs, CIs or tests; small differences (e.g. CA-CLR +3 pp F1) cannot be distinguished from run-to-run noise.
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [A] dataset, code and prompts released (p. 3, p. 13–14); [V] key hyper-parameters reported (p. 7).
- Suggested by us [I]: evaluate GPT-class LLMs and SAST tools on the full PrimeVul test set with VD-S so all families share one metric; add near-duplicate (clone) de-duplication; report variance over seeds/runs.
=== du2026reducing
- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Dataset not released (confidentiality); methods and detailed results in a replication package at https://github.com/LLM4SFPR/static-bug-false-positives-reduction-in-practice (p. 2, p. 11).
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Each LLM query run three times per case with majority vote (p. 6). DL models used as trained on their original datasets (p. 6). Temperature, prompt texts, few-shot example source and context lengths: not reported in the paper (prompts said to be in the replication package, p. 5). [V] IRB approval for the interviews (p. 4).
- Code availability: [V] Replication package (p. 2, p. 11).
- Statistical testing: not reported (no significance tests, CIs or variance across the three runs).
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] N=433 with only 105 TPs (19 for DBZ); no tests; differences of 0.01–0.02 between LLM4PFA backbones are within noise.
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Code and results public, data confidential (p. 2). [I] Cannot be replicated on the same data.
=== dubniczky2025castle
- Data availability (public? link?): [V] https://github.com/CASTLE-Benchmark (p. 1); wrappers public; intermediate vendor reports not shared (p. 9).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): not reported. [A] Repeated evaluations deviate by less than 3% (p. 14); number of repeats not reported.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] 6 vulnerable tests per CWE; differences of a few TPs between tools are within noise; no CIs; LLM run-to-run variance only summarised (<3%).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [I] Dataset and wrappers public with tool versions (p. 1, p. 9, p. 11); LLM settings and API-tool versions missing.
=== fu2023chatgpt
- Data source(s): [V] Big-Vul (Fan et al.) for RQ1–RQ3: 188k C/C++ functions from 348 GitHub projects, 3,754 vulnerabilities across 91 types, vulnerable functions labelled with CWE-ID and CVSS score, vulnerable:benign ratio 1:20 (p. 3). [V] Big-Vul + CVEFixes as pre-processed by Chen et al. for repair: 5.5k vulnerable-function/patch pairs (p. 3).
- Data availability (public? link?): [A] Dataset, prompts and results published at https://github.com/awsm-research/ChatGPT4Vul (p. 1).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): not reported (single point estimates in bar charts).
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No variance, confidence intervals or significance tests; LLM outputs are non-deterministic and only one run is implied.
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [A] Data, prompts and results released (p. 1); [I] model versions and temperature are not stated, and hosted OpenAI models change over time.
- Suggested by us [I]: re-run the prompted-LLM vs fine-tuned comparison on a de-duplicated, temporally split, label-verified benchmark (e.g. PrimeVul), add a SAST baseline, and report variance across repeated LLM runs.
=== gnieciak2025large
- [A] A head-to-head quantitative and qualitative evaluation of three rule-based SAST tools (SonarQube, CodeQL, Snyk Code) and three LLMs on the GitHub Models platform (GPT-4.1, Mistral Large, DeepSeek V3) for vulnerability detection, measuring precision, recall, F1, latency and developer effort (p. 1–2).
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] LLMs accessed via GitHub Models API through the authors' tool ProjectAnalyzer, which concatenates all project files (.cs, .csproj, .sln) into a single prompt and converts the JSON answer to SARIF (p. 5). [V] System prompt asks the model to act as "a static code analysis engine", lists 10 vulnerability types (SQLi, XSS, command injection, insecure deserializat
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] SonarQube, CodeQL, Snyk Code, all run with default configuration settings (p. 4, p. 8). [A] Snyk Code is described as using machine learning, i.e., a hybrid of ML and static analysis (p. 4, p. 9). Model and tool versions: not reported (GitHub Models endpoints named only by model name).
- Data availability (public? link?): [V] ProjectAnalyzer code at https://github.com/Damian0401/ProjectAnalyzer (p. 1). [A] The abstract says an "open benchmark and JSON-based result harness" is released (p. 1); a separate dataset link is not given in the text.
- Code availability: [V] ProjectAnalyzer on GitHub (p. 1).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): not reported. [V] When a tool reported nothing on a project, its precision is recorded as 0.000 and enters the average (e.g., SonarQube S04, S05, S08, S10) (p. 9).
- [A] GPT-4.1 not publicly accessible, hence the use of GitHub Models for equal conditions (p. 5).
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] N = 10 projects, 63 vulns, single runs, no tests or CIs; per-project F1 varies widely (e.g., S04 with 1 vulnerability).
=== guo2025repoaudit
- Sampling / selection method: "well-maintained" projects from prior bug reports [A] (p. 7). The paper says both "ten actively maintained repositories" (p. 2) and "nine open-source GitHub projects" (p. 8, p. 9); Table 4 lists nine [V] (p. 9).
- Data availability (public? link?): code at https://github.com/PurCL/RepoAudit [V] (p. 1). A labelled dataset release is not reported.
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): none; single run per setting (temperature study gives one run per temperature) [V] (p. 17).
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): no tests; one run per configuration; small counts (11 FPs).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): code public (p. 1); prompts partly shown (p. 6, p. 7); full labelled report set not reported.
=== kaniewski2026systematic
- **Version analysed:** arXiv:2507.22659v2 (19 Dec 2025) (p. 1), the preprint of the TOSEM article (DOI 10.1145/3815425), not the typeset journal version. Study statistics are "as of December 13th 2025" (p. 8).
Convention for this survey: two kinds of numbers are marked [V]: counts about the review's own corpus shown in its own tables and figures, and dataset statistics that the authors recomputed from the published datasets (Table 5 states the numbers "are reproduced with the officially published datasets", p. 28). They are the review's own data, although we cannot re-check the extraction. Anything repo
- Data availability: artifacts and the categorised study list are in a public GitHub repository [144] (p. 3, p. 43).
- Code availability: artifacts released [144] (p. 3).
- Statistical testing: none; not reported.
- Statistical conclusion: not applicable (no inferential analysis).
- Reproducibility: strong for an SLR. The full search string is printed (p. 7), and the artifacts and categorised studies are public [144] (p. 3, p. 43). Screening records and QA scores are not reported.
=== khare2025understanding
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] CodeQL with official queries for the Top-25 CWEs, on synthetic datasets only (OWASP, Juliet Java, Juliet C/C++) because real-world projects need building (p. 7–8). [V] DeepDFA (GNN over CFG + dataflow facts) and LineVul (transformer) from DeepDFA's artifact, trained on Juliet C/C++, CVEFixes C/C++ (test samples excluded) or BigVul, 80/20 train/validation, 
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): not reported; [A] "significantly" is used descriptively (p. 1); standard-deviation bars across models in Fig. 2 (p. 5).
4. [V] CWE-DF raises average F1 over CWE and Basic prompts on real-world datasets by up to 0.18 (CVEFixes C/C++) and 0.14 (CVEFixes Java), with lowest variance across models (p. 5). [V] Basic prompt names an incorrect CWE in >60% (Java) and >53% (C/C++) of samples (p. 6; Table VII).
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] 1,000 samples per dataset is reasonable, but per-CWE analysis uses as few as 10 samples (p. 7); no significance tests or CIs; single runs.
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [I] Prompts fully given (p. 14–15) and model versions listed (p. 4); sampled subsets and code not linked in this arXiv version.
=== li2024iris
- Data source(s): [V] CWE-Bench-Java, curated from the GitHub Advisory Database, cross-checked with libraries.io and snyk.io, built with Maven (p. 7, p. 19).
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Funnel 1065 initial CVEs → 430 with GitHub URL/version → 265 with fix commit → 149 compilable → 144 with Java-code fixes → 120 after manual validation by two co-authors who cross-checked each other (p. 19). How the 30 RQ2 projects were chosen: not reported.
- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Dataset and build scripts at https://github.com/iris-sast/cwe-bench-java (p. 2).
- Code availability: [V] https://github.com/iris-sast/iris (p. 1).
- Statistical testing: not reported (no significance tests or confidence intervals; number of runs not reported, settings are deterministic: temperature 0, fixed seed for GPT models, p. 21).
- [I] Number of runs not reported (deterministic settings, p. 21), no variance or significance tests; the 28-detection gap is large, but smaller gaps between LLMs are untested.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No tests, number of runs not reported; N=120 overall but small per-CWE cells (CWE-78 N=13).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Code, dataset, model IDs and hyper-parameters are reported (p. 1, p. 2, p. 20–21). [I] Pinned OpenAI model snapshots may be retired, which limits exact replication.
=== li2026llm
- Data availability (public? link?): artifacts (scripts, prompts, taxonomy labels, statistics) at https://github.com/Feng-Jay/LLM4Security [V] (p. 2).
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: released replication packages of each specialized tool with hyper-parameters from the original papers; no extra timeouts or token/money budgets [V] (p. 6). Default RepoAudit configuration; IRIS/LLMDFA/INFERROI use their own LLM-generated API lists; KNighter checkers generated from 18 bug-fixing patches from its original study [V] (p. 7). General agen
- Code availability: yes, project homepage above [V] (p. 2). Appendices A–C (FP examples, rule lists, detailed cost statistics) are referenced but are not in our 20-page PDF (p. 7, p. 13, p. 15).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): no significance tests between tools. Labelling accuracy estimated with stratified sampling, normal approximation and finite-population correction at the 95% level [V] (p. 11, p. 13); the intervals themselves are not printed in the text we have.
- [I] The low SFDRs of general agents rest on very few warnings (Codex: 2.44 × 9 ≈ 22 C/C++ and 1.47 × 15 ≈ 22 Java warnings), so they are imprecise; no per-tool confidence intervals are shown. Based on Tables VII and IX (p. 11, p. 12).
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): no significance tests between tools; small warning counts for some tools; no run-to-run variance.
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): good — artifacts, prompts and rule lists released (p. 2, p. 7); API model versions may change.
- Suggested by us [I]: an independent (non-evaluated) judge or full manual labelling for warning triage; repeated runs with variance; LLM vs DL vs SAST on the same post-cutoff projects with recall measured via newly disclosed vulnerabilities.
=== risse2025top
- Data availability (public? link?): [A] Scripts, sampled functions, labels and explanations at https://github.com/niklasrisse/TopScoreWrongExam (p. 6–7, p. 13).
- Code availability: [A] GitHub repository above (p. 7).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): not reported beyond Cohen's kappa; no CIs on proportions.
- [I] Word-count GBC vs SOTA compares a model the authors trained with literature numbers produced under possibly different splits and preprocessing (p. 7, p. 11); no re-run of SOTA models on identical splits, no repeated runs, and GBC settings are not given.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] "Context-dependent" is not a measure of detector failure; a context-dependent vulnerability may still be statistically predictable from code patterns. The word-count probe tests exploitability of datasets, not model behaviour.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No CIs; per-dataset proportions from n=100 (vulnerable) and n=30 (secure).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [A] Full artifact (scripts, samples, labels, explanations) released (p. 13).
- Uncertainties: GBC hyper-parameters and the exact train/evaluation splits used for the word-count probe are not stated in the paper text (may be in the artifact). The abstract's ">90% of functions" combines vulnerable (151/151) and secure (82/90) results.
=== sheng2025llms
- Sample size (N) and unit: 58 "highly related" studies, within "more than 80 papers" selected from "over 500" screened (p. 3), or "approximately 500-600" screened (p. 4) [A]. The language statistics are based on "56 selected papers" (p. 10), not 58.
- Time window: 2019–2024 (p. 3). NVD CVE statistics were collected until 3 November 2024 (Table 3, p. 10).
- Data availability: a GitHub list of papers is maintained (p. 1). An extraction sheet is not reported.
- Code availability: not applicable; a paper list is on GitHub (p. 1).
- Statistical testing: none; not reported.
- [I] Weak review methodology. There is no search string, no database list, no formal criteria, no quality appraisal and no PRISMA-style counts (p. 3–4). Its corpus-level statistics are therefore less reliable than those of a protocol-based SLR such as `kaniewski2026systematic`, and the survey should be weighted lower for "state of the field" claims.
  - 58 studies (p. 8) vs 56 papers used for the language statistics (p. 10).
- Statistical conclusion: not applicable; F1 values are listed, not pooled.
=== shu2026evaluating
- Data availability (public? link?): data, training and evaluation scripts on GitHub (SpanShu96/Large-Language-Model-for-Multilingual-Vulnerability-Detection) (p. 48).
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: PLMs replicated following Steenhoek et al. 2024a, using the original authors' hyper-parameters (p. 15, p. 43). LoRA for instruction tuning (p. 14, p. 16). Hardware: Xeon Gold 6342, 512 GB RAM, 2 x A800 GPUs (p. 16). Detailed hyper-parameters (learning rate, epochs, LoRA rank, temperature/decoding) are not reported in the paper; it refers to the repli
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): **none.** No significance tests, confidence intervals or repeated runs/seeds are reported. The words "significantly" and "significant" are used without tests (e.g. p. 21, p. 26, p. 38).
- [I] **The headline result rests on one configuration.** GPT-4o ITFSP is the only LLM setting clearly above chance at function level (next best 0.5874). Few-shot hurts every other model, and the paper gives no explanation, ablation, seed variation or test. A single strong outlier without variance estimates is fragile. Based on Table 3 (p. 17).
- [I] **Possible leakage via paired functions and BM25 retrieval.** The split is random at function level (p. 7), and each vulnerable function has its fixed twin labelled clean (p. 6). Twins and functions from the same CVE/project can fall on opposite sides of the split, and BM25 few-shot retrieval from the training set could then return a near-identical twin with the opposite label. Only exact-ma
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): no tests, confidence intervals or seeds. Many configurations (≈30) are compared on one split, and the best is chosen post hoc. Per-language and per-CWE cells are small (e.g. C# 44/13; CWE-862 n = 1) (p. 7, p. 8, p. 30).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): data and scripts are released (p. 48), and model versions are given for the OpenAI models (p. 15). Hyper-parameters, decoding settings and GPT fine-tuning details are not in the paper (p. 16).
- Version: metadata = EMSE 2026 (DOI 10.1007/s10664-026-10832-4). The analysed text is arXiv 2506.07503v2 (10 Mar 2026), identity matched by arXiv id. The typeset journal version may differ slightly. The running header reads "W. Dong et al.", a template artifact.
=== tan2026think
- Data availability (public? link?): replication package with code, prompts and dataset on Zenodo, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21401826 [V] (p. 5, p. 12).
- Code availability: yes, Zenodo package (p. 12).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): Wilcoxon signed-rank with Cohen's d for RQ1/RQ2 [V] (p. 6, p. 7); Wilcoxon signed-rank with Bonferroni for paired explanation scores, Mann–Whitney for correct vs incorrect, Spearman and partial Spearman for length effects [V] (p. 5, p. 8, p. 9). No confidence intervals reported; the reasoning × orchestration inte
- [A] Deterministic decoding (T = 0) and a single run per configuration: results limited to deterministic decoding, no repeated-run variability (p. 11).
- [I] Statistical tests on 8 or 16 paired configuration-level means have little power and no correction across RQ1/RQ2 tests; differences between individual cells should not be over-read (the authors say this too, p. 6).
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): single runs; small numbers of paired configuration means; Bonferroni applied only in RQ3 (p. 8, p. 9).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): good — open models, vLLM versions, hardware, prompts and replication package on Zenodo (p. 4, p. 12).
- Stated by authors [A]: more reasoning-oriented families (distilled DeepSeek-R1, Gemma) and larger models; costlier repository-level settings with dependency resolution, retrieval and tool support (p. 11); deeper per-model analysis and significance testing of the reasoning × orchestration interaction (p. 8).
=== xiong2026sifting
- Data source(s): [V] OWASP Benchmark for Java v1.2 (synthetic servlets with injected vulnerabilities, labelled) (p. 6); Vul4J (79 reproducible Java vulnerabilities from Project KB, 25 CWEs) (p. 8); OSS-Fuzz/OSV records for 5 C/C++ projects (mpv, libhevc, libical, gpsd, quickjs) with fixing commits 10–12 months after Claude Sonnet 4's training cutoff (p. 9).
- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Scripts and data stated to be public at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18420284 (p. 21). [I] The reference list gives a different Zenodo DOI for the same artifact (10.5281/zenodo.21282004, ref [6], p. 21); which is current is unclear.
- Code availability: [V] Zenodo artifact (p. 21).
- Statistical testing: not reported. [I] The abstract says agents "significantly outperform" vanilla prompting (p. 1), but no significance test is reported; Cohen's κ is the only statistic.
- [I] Real-world Java (N=50) and C/C++ (N=50) samples are small; per-cell differences of a few alerts change the percentages a lot, and no confidence intervals are given.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No tests, many configurations compared, small real-world N, apparently single runs.
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Tool versions, model IDs and artifact are given (p. 6–7, p. 21). [I] Two different Zenodo DOIs are listed.
=== yildiz2025benchmarking
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): none reported.
- [A] Missing statistics such as the share of interprocedural vulnerabilities; annotation hard to scale (p. 9).
- [I] No repeated runs, variance or significance tests; differences of a few points (e.g. 0.1-point pAcc gain) are not interpretable. Based on p. 6–7.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): no tests, no variance, many configurations compared.
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): code and data released (p. 2); prompts in Appendix A (p. 12, p. 13).
=== zhou2024comparison
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] SAST, all free/open-source: Java — CodeQL, Contrast Codesec Scan, Horusec, Insider, SpotBugs, Semgrep, SonarQube CE; C — Flawfinder, Cppcheck, Infer, CodeChecker, CodeQL; Python — Bandit, Dlint, DevSkim, CodeQL, Graudit, Semgrep (p. 4). [V] Commercial LLMs excluded from the main study because of cost and non-reproducibility (p. 4); a small side experiment 
- Data source(s): [V] Java from Li et al. (SAST study for Java), C from Lipp et al. (static C analyzers study), both real-world CVEs whose repositories were re-downloaded; new Python dataset built from NVD 2002–2023 entries linked to GitHub fix commits (p. 3).
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Repositories kept only if downloadable via the GitHub API (Java) or per the original authors' instructions (C); Python projects that errored during SAST scanning were omitted (p. 3). [V] Vulnerable functions = pre-fix versions of functions changed by the fix commit; all other functions labelled non-vulnerable (p. 3–4). [V] Random 8:1:1 train/validation/test split
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): not reported; single runs, no variance or CIs. [V] A rank-sum heuristic (rank by S2 + rank by marked ratio) picks the "best" approach (p. 8).
- [I] Very small test sets: detection ratios are multiples of ~10–12.5 points (Table 3, p. 6), so each language result rests on about 8–10 CVEs; one CVE moves a ratio by 10+ points. No variance, repeated splits or CIs. Most cross-tool differences are therefore statistically unreliable.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] ~8–10 test CVEs per language, single run, no tests; many comparisons across 15 tools × 12 LLMs × 4 adaptations.
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [I] Hyper-parameters reported (p. 5, p. 7); code/data claimed public without a link (p. 10); SAST configuration missing.

=== zhou2025large
- Statistical testing: none (descriptive review); not reported.
- Statistical conclusion: not applicable (no quantitative synthesis).
- Reproducibility: keywords are in an online appendix (p. 5). Extraction data and QA scores are not released (not reported).

But Table 2 implies about 14.3% vulnerable lines (25,161 / 175,768) (p. 8). 810 test functions x 113 padded line slots ≈ 91,53

content.content:
## 7. Key findings
1. C/C++ controlled set: general agents average recall 59.55% (131/220) and precision 32.19% (131/407); KNighter detects 0 vulnerabilities in all three CWEs; RepoAudit with its original backbone (Claude Sonnet 3.5) detects 0 of 110 (0 TPs among 40 warnings: 0 warnings on CWE-401, 33 on CWE-416, 7 on CWE-476), and RepoAudit (GPT-5.4) detects 2 (CWE-476 recall 5.71%) — [V] (p. 7, Table IV).
   - Table XII lists a minimum of 0.00K input tokens and $0.00 for both RepoAudit variants on the real-world projects — [V] (p. 16). [I] So on at least one project RepoAudit made no LLM call at all; this fits the authors' finding that incomplete API modelling explains all 108/108 RepoAudit (GPT-5.4) misses (p. 7), i.e. sources/sinks were never matched. Relevant to the guo2025repoaudit tension (§9).
2. C/C++ per CWE (Table IV): CWE-401 Codex R 68.00% / P 41.98%, Claude Code R 80.00% / P 40.00%, CodeQL R 6.00% / P 14.29%, Semgrep and CSA 0%; CWE-416 Codex R 40.00%, Claude Code R 36.00%, CodeQL/Semgrep/CSA 0%; CWE-476 Codex R 62.86%, Claude Code R 45.71%, CodeQL R 34.29% with 1,110 warnings (P 1.08%) — [V] (p. 7).
3. Java controlled set: Codex average recall 63.87% (99/155), Claude Code 81.94% (127/155); CodeQL 14.19%, Semgrep 6.67%, SpotBugs 14.84%; LLMDFA (GPT-5.4) finds 1 vulnerability; INFERROI (GPT-5.4) reaches 66.00% recall on CWE-772 vs CodeQL 10.00% and SpotBugs 6.00% — [V] (p. 9, Table VI p. 10).
4. Java precision is low for most tools (e.g. CWE-022: IRIS GPT-4 6.30%, Semgrep 0.29% from 2,075 warnings, SpotBugs 1.76%, Codex 58.73%, Claude Code 37.29%) — [V] (p. 10, Table VI).
5. Swapping in GPT-5.4 barely changes recall of specialized methods but raises some precision (IRIS CWE-078 6.06% → 20.00%; INFERROI 15.74% → 20.50%) — [V] (p. 9). The authors conclude that the workflow, not the model, limits recall (e.g. RepoAudit GPT-5.4 vs Codex on the same model) — [A] (p. 9).
6. Incomplete API modelling and incomplete candidate exploration explain 108/108 (RepoAudit GPT-5.4), 97/110 (KNighter GPT-5.4), 40/44 (Codex) and 40/45 (Claude Code) missed C/C++ vulnerabilities — [V] (p. 7). With perfect allocation/deallocation API specs on CWE-401, recall rises: RepoAudit 0 → 48%, Codex 68 → 90%, Claude Code 80 → 96%, CodeQL 6 → 56% — [V] (p. 8, Table V).
7. Vulnerabilities missed by general agents sit in larger files than detected ones (Fig. 4 C/C++, Fig. 6 Java) — [V] (p. 9, p. 10). The authors attribute this to file size and complexity, and say IRIS and INFERROI are largely unaffected because they reason over compact representations such as CFGs — [A] (p. 8, p. 10).
8. LLM-based tools contribute most unique detections; traditional tools add few unique ones (CodeQL at most 3 unique on CWE-022) — [V] (p. 9, p. 10, Fig. 5).
9. Real-world C/C++ (Table VII): overall SFDR RepoAudit (Sonnet 3.5) 92.77%, KNighter (o3-mini) 81.25%, Codex 9.09% (2.44 warnings/project), Claude Code 74.07%, CodeQL 86.01% (752.67 warnings/project; 6,345 on gpac), Semgrep 100.00%, CSA 85.51% — [V] (p. 11). GPT-5.4 versions: RepoAudit 95.41%, KNighter 95.56% (Table VIII) — [V] (p. 11).
10. Real-world Java (Table IX): IRIS (GPT-4) 97.80% SFDR with 232.42 warnings/project, LLMDFA 100.00%, INFERROI 96.40%, Codex 31.82% (1.47 warnings/project), Claude Code 81.82%, CodeQL 77.00%, Semgrep 92.71%, SpotBugs 86.21%; traditional tools emit warnings in only about half of projects — [V] (p. 12). IRIS with GPT-5.4 drops to 78.73% (Table X) — [V] (p. 12).
11. Codex labels were 94.36% accurate on 621 manually validated warnings (population-weighted 98.16%); Codex FP-reason labels 87.76% accurate on 425 cases (weighted 92.52%) — [V] (p. 11, p. 13).
12. FP root causes: incorrect program-point classification B1 = 63.33% (3,734/5,896) and truncated interprocedural context A1 = 14.60% (861/5,896); LLM tools additionally show incorrect control flow (A2), missed sanitizers/guards (D1, >15% in 7 of 12 LLM settings) and prompt deviations (C1) — [V] (p. 15, Table XI p. 14). CodeQL's largest FP causes are A1 35.80% and path-insensitivity D3 20.17% — [V] (p. 14).
13. Cost (Table XII): RepoAudit (Sonnet 3.5) up to 225,493.97K input and 38,078.26K output tokens and $1,247.66 for one project, average $172.77; LLMDFA (GPT-4) average $61.60 and 2,000 min per Java project (max 4,638 min); IRIS (GPT-4) average $2.59, 213.44 min; INFERROI average $11.62–$12.99; KNighter $0.34–$2.36; Codex $5.38 / 14.80 min; Claude Code $9.67 / 13.19 min per project. SAST average runtimes 0.64 (Semgrep) to 60.92 (CSA) minutes, no token cost — [V] (p. 16).
14. Per warning: Codex $2.93 and 8.1 min, Claude Code $1.77 and 2.4 min; LLMDFA >$24 and >800 min per warning — [V] (p. 15, p. 16).

## 7. Key findings
1. Non-agent: thinking beats instruct F1 in 7 of 8 model–prompt settings; mean F1 0.31 → 0.41 (Wilcoxon p = 0.023, Cohen's d = 1.37); accuracy barely changes (0.518 vs 0.523, p = 0.46), so the gain is a recall shift — [V] (p. 6).
2. Best non-agent F1: Nemotron-Super-49B thinking zero-shot F1 0.620 (recall 0.749, precision 0.529); best non-agent P-C: Qwen3-30B-A3B instruct zero-shot 22.5% — [V] (p. 6, Table 2). Nemotron-Nano-8B stays weak (zero-shot recall 0.005–0.048) — [V] (p. 6).
3. Thinking improves P-C in 6 of 8 non-agent settings — [V] (p. 6).
4. Agent designs (means over 16 settings): SA F1 0.368 / recall 0.326 / P-C 13.7; DA F1 0.634 / recall 0.885 / precision 0.502 / P-C 6.2; MA F1 0.497 / recall 0.559 / P-C 15.8 — [V] (p. 7, Table 3).
5. DA flags 88.2% of functions (PPR 0.882, FPR 0.880) vs SA 30.3% (FPR 0.280) and MA 55.4% (FPR 0.549); DA vs SA F1 p < 0.0001, d = 1.40; MA vs SA p = 0.0013, d = 0.92 — [V] (p. 7).
6. DA beats SA on F1 in all 16 settings and is the most stable (CV 9% vs MA 32%, SA 46%); MA has the best P-C in 11 of 16 settings, DA in none — [V] (p. 7, p. 8).
7. Thinking's F1 benefit reverses with orchestration: ΔF1 +0.104 (NA), +0.100 (SA), −0.054 (DA), −0.066 (MA); ΔP-C stays positive (+1.9, +1.5, +8.1, +5.4) — [V] (p. 8, Table 5).
8. Call-matched (193 pairs, zero-shot, 2 models): 4-call self-revision has the highest mean P-C (24.7) vs SA and MA (21.9) and DA (4.7), with FPR 0.47 vs DA 0.93; the authors conclude much of the multi-agent benefit is extra inference budget — [V]/[A] (p. 11, Table 9).
9. Cost: thinking uses 2.7–4.4× more energy and 2.5–3.6× more output tokens; MA-thinking averages 25,533 tokens per sample vs 3,703 for NA; per configuration SA $27.5 / 8.0 h, DA $37.1 / 11.5 h, MA $52.7 / 14.4 h; all 64 configurations cost about $2,448, 481 kWh and 423.0M tokens — [V] (p. 10, Table 8).

def cmd_scaffold(a):
    d = project_dir(a.project)
    tpl = (TEMPLATES / "paper-analysis.md").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    for meta in selected(d, a.keys):
        f = d / "papers" / meta["key"] / "analysis.md"
        if f.exists():
            print(f"EXISTS {meta['key']}/analysis.md (not overwritten)")
            continue
        authors = "; ".join(f"{x.get('family')}, {x.get('given')}".strip(", ") for x in meta.get("authors", [])[:6])
        ft = meta.get("fulltext") or {}
        f.write_text(tpl.replace("{{KEY}}", meta["key"]).replace("{{TITLE}}", meta.get("title") or "")
                     .replace("{{AUTHORS}}", authors).replace("{{YEAR}}", str(meta.get("year") or ""))
                     .replace("{{VENUE}}", meta.get("venue") or "").replace("{{VENUE_KIND}}", meta.get("venue_kind") or "")
                     .replace("{{DOI}}", meta.get("doi") or "none").replace("{{URL}}", meta.get("url") or "")
                     .replace("{{BASIS}}", "full-text" if ft.get("status") in ("downloaded", "user-supplied") else "abstract-only")
                     .replace("{{DATE}}", today()), encoding="utf-8")
        print(f"CREATED {meta['key']}/analysis.md")
    refresh(d)


def cmd_cite_check(a):
    """Every [@key, p. N] must name a project paper, a page that exists, and no retracted paper."""
    d = project_dir(a.project)
    papers = {m["key"]: m for m in load_papers(d)}
    bad = 0
    for f in map(Path, a.files):
        text = f.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        cites = [(k, p) for grp in re.findall(r"\[([^\[\]]*@[^\[\]]*)\]", text)
                 for k, p in re.findall(r"(?<![\w.])@([A-Za-z][\w:-]*)(?:,\s*pp?\.\s*(\d+))?", grp)]
        own = papers.get(f.parent.name) if f.name == "analysis.md" else None
        if own:  # analyses cite their own paper as (p. N)
            cites += [(own["key"], p) for p in re.findall(r"\(pp?\.\s*(\d+)", text)]
        for k, p in cites:
            m = papers.get(k)
            if not m:
                print(f"UNKNOWN KEY  {f.name}: @{k} is not a paper in this project")
                bad += 1
                continue
            if m.get("is_retracted"):
                print(f"RETRACTED    {f.name}: @{k} is retracted")
                bad += 1
            pages = (m.get("fulltext") or {}).get("pages")
            if p and pages and int(p) > pages:
                print(f"BAD PAGE     {f.name}: @{k} p. {p} but the PDF has {pages} pages")
                bad += 1
        print(f"{f.name}: {len(cites)} citations of {len({k for k, _ in cites})} papers")
    print("cite-check: OK" if not bad else f"cite-check: {bad} problem(s)")
    return 1 if bad else 0


def cmd_index(a):
    targets = [project_dir(a.project)] if a.project else [RESEARCH / p["id"] for p in load_registry()["projects"]]
    for d in targets:
        if d.exists():
            print(f"{d.name}: {refresh(d)}")


def cmd_log(a):
    d = project_dir(a.project)
    log_event(d, a.phase, a.message)
    print("logged")


def cmd_doctor(a):
    ok = True

    def check(cond, label, hint=""):
        nonlocal ok
        ok &= bool(cond)
        print(f"[{'ok' if cond else 'MISSING'}] {label}" + ("" if cond else f"  -> {hint}"))
    check(sys.version_info >= (3, 9), f"python {sys.version.split()[0]} (>=3.9)")

# Methodology comparison — LLM-based vs traditional static analysis and deep learning for source-code vulnerability detection

- Project: `2026-11-12-llm-based-vs-traditional-static-analysis`
- Date: 2026-11-12
- Inputs: 20 analyses (`status: complete`, all full text), `evidence-matrix.md`, `literature-matrix.md`, critical reviews A and B of 2026-11-12.
- Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data, **[A]** author claim, **[I]** our interpretation. Unlabelled numeric statements are [V] from the cited page.
- Source tiers: three items are recorded by `rlab` as arXiv preprints. IRIS [@li2024iris, p. 1] and RepoAudit [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 1] are the ICLR 2025 and ICML 2025 camera-ready texts. Only zhou2024comparison is a true preprint without a known peer-reviewed version (**not peer-reviewed**) [@zhou2024comparison, p. 1]. Nine further papers were read in their arXiv versions, not the version of record (see §5, W9).

A short glossary for readers new to the area: *SAST* (static application security testing) tools such as CodeQL or Semgrep scan code with hand-written rules. *DL detectors* (e.g. LineVul, Devign) are neural networks trained on labelled vulnerable code. A *balanced* test set has 50% vulnerable samples. *Pairwise correctness (P-C / pAcc)* is the share of vulnerable/patched function pairs where both versions are classified correctly. *SFDR* is the sampled false discovery rate, i.e. the share of a tool's warnings that are false.

## 2. Approach families

| Family | Papers | Typical strengths | Typical weaknesses |
|---|---|---|---|
| A. Head-to-head LLM vs SAST | gnieciak2025large, dubniczky2025castle, khare2025understanding, zhou2024comparison, li2026llm | Same targets for both families; directly answers RQ1 | Small or synthetic targets, SAST on default rules, unequal scoring, single runs |
| B. LLM vs fine-tuned DL / PLM | fu2023chatgpt, ding2025vulnerability, chakraborty2024revisiting, khare2025understanding, shu2026evaluating, zhou2024comparison, du2026reducing | Large N; standard metrics; trivial baselines sometimes reported | Noisy function-level C/C++ datasets; F1 on balanced data; no SAST arm except khare and zhou2024 |
| C1. Hybrid: LLM inside the analyser (spec inference, dataflow) | li2024iris, guo2025repoaudit; independently re-evaluated in li2026llm | Real projects; builds on mature analysers; new bugs found | Evaluated by tool authors on chosen targets; recall rarely measured |
| C2. Hybrid: LLM filters SAST alarms | du2026reducing, xiong2026sifting | Large false-alarm reduction; cost per alarm measured | True vulnerabilities also filtered; small real-world samples |
| D. Agentic / reasoning LLMs | tan2026think, yildiz2025benchmarking, ahmed2026secvuleval, li2026llm (general agents), xiong2026sifting | Repository context and tool use; controlled factorial designs (tan) | Cost; gains often explained by more inference or more flagging |
| E. Benchmark-realism studies | chakraborty2024revisiting, ding2025vulnerability, risse2025top, ahmed2026secvuleval, yildiz2025benchmarking, dubniczky2025castle, li2024iris | Audit labels and leakage; build better benchmarks | Mostly C/C++; some audits are second-hand |
| F. Surveys | kaniewski2026systematic, sheng2025llms, zhou2025large | Field-wide view of datasets and methods | No performance meta-analysis; overlap with primary studies |

**A. Head-to-head LLM vs SAST.** Results depend on the unit of analysis. On small, self-contained targets, prompted frontier LLMs score above SAST: macro F1 0.75–0.80 vs 0.26–0.55 on C# projects [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10]; CASTLE score 977 for GPT-o3-mini vs 661 for the best non-LLM tool [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11]. On function-level synthetic suites, CodeQL has higher accuracy than the best LLM on all three datasets [@khare2025understanding, p. 9]. At repository level, LLMs detect more CVEs but mark up to 77.4% of functions [@zhou2024comparison, p. 7]. General coding agents reach far higher recall than SAST [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 9]. [I] The family's main weakness is that each study uses its own targets and scoring, so the papers measure different things (see §3.5).

**B. LLM vs fine-tuned DL/PLM.** On random-split Big-Vul, fine-tuned small models clearly beat prompted ChatGPT (F1 94% vs 29%) [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4]. Under realistic splits all models collapse [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7; @chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 7]. The only multilingual comparison finds that the winner depends on class balance [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40]. [I] This family inherits the label noise and leakage of Big-Vul-type data (§5, W2).

**C1. Hybrid detection (LLM inside the analyser).** IRIS doubles CodeQL's detections on CWE-Bench-Java (55 vs 27 of 120), with AvgFDR 84.82% vs 90.03% [@li2024iris, p. 8]. Only GPT-4 lowers FDR below CodeQL; smaller LLMs worsen it [@li2024iris, p. 10]. RepoAudit reports 78.43% precision [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 8]. Both look much weaker in li2026llm's independent re-evaluation (§4, C2 and C6).

**C2. Hybrid false-positive filtering.** The industrial LLM4PFA hybrid removes 94–98% of false alarms while keeping 75–88% of real bugs [@du2026reducing, p. 8]. The best agent configuration cuts OWASP FPR from 98.3% to 6.3% [@xiong2026sifting, p. 12] but drops 22.25% of true vulnerabilities [@xiong2026sifting, p. 18]. [I] This is the most consistent benefit in the corpus, but it is a trade-off, not a free gain (§3.7).

**D. Agentic/reasoning LLMs.** Thinking mode raises F1 mainly through recall (0.31 → 0.41) at 2.7–4.4× the energy [@tan2026think, p. 6; @tan2026think, p. 10]. A four-call self-revision matches the multi-agent pipeline on P-C, so much of the agent gain is extra inference budget [@tan2026think, p. 11] [A]. ReAct agents give the best pairwise accuracy with GPT-4o models, but it stays ≤20.17% [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 6].

**E. Benchmark realism.** Manual audits find only 39–65% of vulnerable labels correct in BigVul, Devign and DiverseVul [@risse2025top, p. 8], and 24–36% in CodeXGLUE/Devign and VulnPatchPairs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4]. A word-count classifier reaches F1 0.86 on BigVul [@risse2025top, p. 11]. Statement-level scoring halves LLM F1 [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8].

**F. Surveys.** Two SLRs and one narrative survey describe a field dominated by function-level C/C++ classification on noisy datasets [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 26; @zhou2025large, p. 18; @sheng2025llms, p. 20]. None pools effect sizes. kaniewski2026systematic excludes studies that only post-process tool output [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 8], so it does not cover family C2.

## 3. Comparable results

Numbers are compared only where dataset, metric and setup match.

| Comparison | Dataset / metric | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 3.1 CodeQL on OWASP Benchmark (khare vs xiong) | OWASP Java; P/R/F1 | **Comparable** (different sample size) |
| 3.2 PrimeVul pairs (ding, tan, yildiz) | PrimeVul-derived pairs; P-C / pAcc | **Partly comparable** |
| 3.3 Big-Vul F1 (fu, ding, chakraborty, risse) | "Big-Vul"; F1 | **Not comparable** |
| 3.4 CodeQL on CWE-Bench-Java (li2024iris vs li2026llm) | Java CVEs; recall | **Partly comparable** |
| 3.5 LLM-vs-SAST headline scores | different units and metrics | **Not comparable** |
| 3.6 LLM filtering of SAST alarms (du vs xiong) | different alarms and metrics | **Not numerically comparable** |

**3.1 CodeQL on OWASP (comparable).** khare reports CodeQL P 0.58, R 0.96, F1 0.72 on a 1,000-snippet balanced OWASP sample [@khare2025understanding, p. 9]. xiong reports P 60.3%, R 97.0%, F1 74.4% on the full 2,740-case OWASP v1.2 [@xiong2026sifting, p. 11]. [I] Two independent groups agree within about 2 points. This is the only cross-paper SAST figure we can treat as replicated. Both describe a high-recall, low-precision tool (FPR 68.2% [@xiong2026sifting, p. 11]) whose F1 is near the always-vulnerable value of 0.667 on balanced data.

**3.2 PrimeVul pairs (partly comparable).** All three studies use pairs of vulnerable and patched functions drawn from PrimeVul:
- ding: GPT-4 CoT P-C 12.94% on 564 test pairs, below a random reference of 22.70% [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9].
- tan: best non-agent P-C 22.5% on 435 pairs with open models [@tan2026think, p. 6]; self-revision 24.7 on 193 pairs [@tan2026think, p. 11].
- yildiz: GPT-4o/4o-mini pAcc 1.02–20.17% on 879 CVE pairs from JITVul, with repository context [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 6].

The pair subsets, models, context and dates differ. [I] The direction agrees: GPT-class and open LLMs stay at or below the ~25% ceiling that independent random labelling can reach. One outlier exists: DeepSeek-Coder-V2 with dependency augmentation reaches pAcc 69.24, reported in an appendix only [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 15]. All three use one dataset family, so this is related evidence, not independent replication.

**3.3 Big-Vul F1 (not comparable).** Reported F1 on "Big-Vul" varies widely:
- CodeBERT: 87% [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4] vs 62.88% [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7].
- Replicated LineVul: 90% [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 6].
- Literature SOTA (DeepDFA): 96.46% [@risse2025top, p. 7].
- Word-count baseline: 0.86 [@risse2025top, p. 11].

Splits, preprocessing and de-duplication differ. [I] A spread of about 25 points for one model on one named dataset means Big-Vul F1 values should be cited only as a range. Because a word-count baseline reaches 0.86, high Big-Vul F1 is not evidence of vulnerability understanding.

**3.4 CodeQL on CWE-Bench-Java (partly comparable).** CodeQL detects 27 of 120 CVEs (22.5%) in the IRIS paper [@li2024iris, p. 8] and has 14.19% recall on li2026llm's Java set [@li2026llm, p. 9]. That set mixes a Maven-only CWE-Bench-Java subset with 50 JLeaks resource leaks [@li2026llm, p. 5]. [I] Both values are low, and the gap is plausibly due to the different CWE mix and CodeQL versions.

**3.5 LLM-vs-SAST headline numbers (not comparable).** gnieciak counts LLM findings as true positives even when the line or column is wrong, which SAST tools are not allowed [@gnieciak2025large, p. 6]. dubniczky uses a severity-weighted score [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 10]. khare uses function-level accuracy on balanced sets [@khare2025understanding, p. 9]. zhou2024 uses CVE detection ratio and marked-function ratio [@zhou2024comparison, p. 5]. li2026llm uses recall on known CVEs and SFDR on new code [@li2026llm, p. 11]. [I] These five studies cannot be pooled or ranked against each other.

**3.6 False-positive filtering (not numerically comparable).** du measures removal of false alarms on 433 industrial alarms of general bug types [@du2026reducing, p. 8]. xiong measures residual FPR and TP miss rate on OWASP and 100 sampled alerts [@xiong2026sifting, p. 12; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18]. Only the qualitative pattern can be compared (§3.7, G6).

### 3.7 Agreements / converging evidence

- **G1. Realistic evaluation collapses reported performance (strong).** Several studies show it:
  - DL precision falls to 1–10% on Real-Vul [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 7].
  - Code-LM F1 falls from 62.88–68.26% (BigVul) to 18.05–21.43% within PrimeVul and 1.91–5.82% cross-dataset [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7].
  - LLM accuracy is 10.5% lower on real-world than synthetic data [@khare2025understanding, p. 5].
  - GPT-4o line-level F1 drops from 0.6641 to 0.3450 on 2024–25 code [@shu2026evaluating, p. 39].
  - Statement-level scoring halves F1 [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8].

  The surveys agree [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 39; @sheng2025llms, p. 20].
- **G2. Benchmark labels are noisy (strong).** Two independent audits find 39–65% [@risse2025top, p. 8] and 24–36% [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4] of vulnerable labels correct. ReVeal has 15% label inconsistency [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 3]. The 25% BigVul figure is Chen et al.'s, reproduced by Ding [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4]; it is not an independent estimate.
- **G3. Prompted LLMs over-flag and cannot separate vulnerable from patched code (moderate).**
  - GPT-4 two-shot calls both versions vulnerable in 71.63% of pairs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9].
  - "Both vulnerable" accounts for 40–95% of LLM failures [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 8].
  - The dual-agent design flags 88.2% of functions [@tan2026think, p. 7].
  - Several of khare's best F1 rows are "always vulnerable" outputs [@khare2025understanding, p. 16].
  - Frontier models over-flag CWE-476/416/190 [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 13] [A].

  [I] ding, yildiz and tan share PrimeVul, so this is partly one dataset family.
- **G4. SAST recall is low on real code and high only on synthetic suites (moderate).** On real code:
  - Best single SAST tools detect 30.0–44.4% of CVEs, and many detect 0% [@zhou2024comparison, p. 6].
  - CodeQL recall is 6.00–34.29% on C/C++ and 14.19% on Java [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 9].
  - CodeQL finds 27/120 on CWE-Bench-Java [@li2024iris, p. 8].
  - On CASTLE, CodeQL reaches 29% and the SAST average is 23% [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 12].

  On synthetic suites, CodeQL reaches accuracy 0.94 on Juliet Java [@khare2025understanding, p. 9].
- **G5. Missing context is the shared failure cause (moderate).**
  - All 151 truly vulnerable audited functions need context beyond the function [@risse2025top, p. 9].
  - LLMs identify required context in ≤41.33% of cases per context type [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 9].
  - Global context is the main failure cause on real C/C++ [@khare2025understanding, p. 7] [A].
  - Incomplete API modelling explains 108/108 RepoAudit (GPT-5.4) misses [@li2026llm, p. 7], and 14.60% of all FPs come from truncated inter-procedural context [@li2026llm, p. 15].
- **G6. LLM false-alarm filtering trades large FP reduction for lost true positives (moderate).** Evidence: du2026reducing reaches 94–98% false-alarm removal with real-bug recall of 0.75–0.88 [@du2026reducing, p. 8]; xiong2026sifting cuts FPR to 6.3% but misses 22.25% of true vulnerabilities [@xiong2026sifting, p. 12; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18]. du covers non-security bug classes, evaluates its authors' own method and has Tencent-affiliated authors [@du2026reducing, p. 1]. Strength is therefore moderate.
- **G7. Prompt-only LLMs trail adapted models (moderate).**
  - Prompted ChatGPT lags fine-tuned models on Big-Vul [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4].
  - GPT-3.5 prompting detects 3.7–23.2% vs 89.2% for fine-tuned CodeBERT [@zhou2024comparison, p. 10].
  - Prompt-only LLMs are near chance on REEF, and only fine-tuned GPT-4o with few-shot stands out [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17].
- **G8. LLM cost far exceeds SAST cost and varies by orders of magnitude (moderate).** SAST runs in minutes with no token cost, while RepoAudit averages $172.77 per project [@li2026llm, p. 16]. Alarm filtering costs cents per alarm [@du2026reducing, p. 8; @xiong2026sifting, p. 17]. Instruction tuning GPT-4o costs about 15× a local PLM training run [@shu2026evaluating, p. 42].

## 4. Contradictions

**C1. Fine-tuned models vs GPT-4: fu2023chatgpt vs ding2025vulnerability.**
- Claim A: fine-tuned AIBugHunter (F1 94%) and CodeBERT (87%) far outperform prompted gpt-4 (29%) [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4].
- Claim B: GPT-4 CoT has a higher P-C (12.94%) than every fine-tuned model (≤3.01%) [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9].
- Differences:
  - metric: F1 vs pairwise correctness;
  - data: noisy random-split Big-Vul at 1:20 vs de-duplicated, time-split PrimeVul pairs;
  - time: 2023 vs 2024 GPT versions.
- Ding's own BigVul rows (F1 62.88–68.26%) agree with Fu's direction [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7].
- [I] Explanation: fine-tuned models probably exploit dataset artefacts that random splits reward and paired, de-duplicated tests remove [@risse2025top, p. 11]. On pairs, GPT-4's edge comes from flagging both versions less uniformly, but it is still below random (22.70%). Neither side shows real detection skill on PrimeVul pairs.

**C2. RepoAudit: guo2025repoaudit vs li2026llm.**
- Claim A: 40 TP / 11 FP (78.43% precision) on 15 C/C++ projects, all 21 known bugs reproduced, $2.54 and 0.44 h per project [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 7; @guo2025repoaudit, p. 8].
- Claim B: in li2026llm, RepoAudit (Sonnet 3.5) detects 0 of 110 known C/C++ vulnerabilities [@li2026llm, p. 7]. On real projects it has 92.77% SFDR [@li2026llm, p. 11] and costs $172.77 on average, up to $1,247.66 per project [@li2026llm, p. 16].
- Differences:
  - targets: prior tools' bug reports vs ReposVul CVEs;
  - code version: older commits vs current HEAD (the five overlapping Linux/ImageMagick modules are in li's real-world set only);
  - metric: precision on own reports vs recall/SFDR;
  - labeller: authors vs Codex;
  - scale: avg 251 KLoC vs multi-million-LOC modules.
- [I] Explanation: RepoAudit depends on source/sink API coverage. li2026llm records zero-token runs and 108/108 misses due to API modelling [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 16], so the tool may perform well only on targets matching its built-in specifications. Neither paper alone settles this.

**C3. "LLMs beat SAST" vs "SAST beats LLMs" vs repository level.**
- Claim A: LLMs win on 10 small C# projects [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10] and on CASTLE C micro-programs [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11].
- Claim B: CodeQL beats the best LLM in accuracy on OWASP, Juliet Java and Juliet C/C++ [@khare2025understanding, p. 9].
- Claim C (repository level): LLMs detect more but mark up to 77.4% of functions [@zhou2024comparison, p. 7]. General agents reach the highest recall, while specialised LLM detectors and SAST both have near-zero recall on some CWEs and 75–100% SFDR [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11].
- Differences: language (C#, C, Java), unit (project, program, function, repository), scoring (lenient LLM location rule in gnieciak [@gnieciak2025large, p. 6]; the CASTLE prompt reveals the scoring rule to the LLM [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 9]), and synthetic vs real code.
- [I] Explanation: synthetic suites match SAST rule sets, while small self-contained programs fit inside an LLM's context. Real repositories defeat both families through missing API and context models (G4, G5). The answer depends on setting and metric, so there is no single winner.

**C4. Does reasoning reduce false positives?**
- Claim A: reasoning models "consistently produced fewer false positives" [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 14]. RepoAudit precision rises to 82.35–88.46% with reasoning backbones [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 16].
- Claim B:
  - In CASTLE's own table, DeepSeek R1 has 166 FP vs GPT-4o's 116 [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11].
  - Thinking mode raises F1 through recall with unchanged accuracy, and its F1 benefit turns negative under dual- and multi-agent designs [@tan2026think, p. 6; @tan2026think, p. 8].
  - Reasoning LLMs are near chance on REEF (Acc 0.52–0.53) [@shu2026evaluating, p. 37].
- Differences: OpenAI o-series vs open reasoning models; micro-benchmark and repository agent vs balanced function pairs; FP count vs F1 and accuracy.
- [I] Explanation: the claim holds for some proprietary reasoning models in some settings and does not generalise to "reasoning" as such.

**C5. Class balance flips the ranking (shu2026evaluating, internal).**
- Claim A: on balanced REEF, fine-tuned GPT-4o + few-shot beats CodeT5P (Acc 0.7196 vs 0.6037; MCC 0.4360 vs 0.2860) [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17].
- Claim B: on the imbalanced (~17% vulnerable) test, PLMs win (UniXcoder F1 0.4626, CodeT5P MCC 0.3627 vs GPT-4o F1 0.4010, MCC 0.2774) [@shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @shu2026evaluating, p. 41].
- yildiz shows the same sensitivity: F1 falls from ~49–65% on balanced pairs to 5.41–12.21% on non-paired PrimeVul [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7].
- [I] Explanation: LLMs flag positives more liberally, which balanced sets reward. Rankings from balanced benchmarks should not be carried over to deployment, where vulnerable code is rare.

**C6. Hybrid IRIS: original vs independent evaluation.**
- Claim A: IRIS+GPT-4 beats CodeQL on 120 Java CVEs (55 vs 27 detected; AvgFDR 84.82% vs 90.03%) [@li2024iris, p. 8].
- Claim B: on 15 real-world Java projects, IRIS (GPT-4) has 97.80% SFDR vs 77.00% for CodeQL [@li2026llm, p. 12].
- Differences: known CVEs vs new code, detections vs SFDR, CodeQL-protocol FDR vs Codex-labelled sampling.
- [I] Explanation: hybrids may raise recall on benchmark CVEs while adding noise on unseen projects. The comparison is not like-for-like, so the tension stays open.

## 5. Methodological weaknesses across the field

- **W1. F1 on balanced data without a trivial baseline.** On a 50/50 set, "flag everything" scores F1 0.667. Examples:
  - shu's DummyClf_vul scores 0.6693 against a best of 0.7075 [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17].
  - tan's best F1 is 0.665–0.666 [@tan2026think, p. 7; @tan2026think, p. 11].
  - All of yildiz's GPT F1 values (48–66) are at or below it [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 6].
  - khare's best-per-dataset F1s include always-vulnerable rows [@khare2025understanding, p. 16].

  [I] Only shu reports the baseline itself.
- **W2. Label noise and leakage.** Exact-copy test-to-train leakage reaches 12.7% (BigVul) and 18.9% (CVEFixes) [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4]. Benchmarks probably sit in LLM pre-training data [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 30] [A]. Only xiong and li2026llm test explicitly on post-cutoff code [@xiong2026sifting, p. 15; @li2026llm, p. 5]. shu adds a time split [@shu2026evaluating, p. 39].
- **W3. LLM-as-labeller.** li2026llm labels real-world warnings with Codex, a tool it also evaluates (94.36% accurate on 621 validated warnings) [@li2026llm, p. 11]. tan's LLM judge rates explanations higher in ways humans corroborate only for informativeness [@tan2026think, p. 8]. [I] Self-labelling can favour the labelling model.
- **W4. Unequal scoring between LLMs and SAST.** gnieciak applies a lenient location rule only to LLMs [@gnieciak2025large, p. 6]. CASTLE's LLM prompt states the reward and penalty scheme [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 9]. SAST tools run on default configurations [@gnieciak2025large, p. 8], and khare tests CodeQL only on synthetic data [@khare2025understanding, p. 7]. [I] These choices favour LLMs in two studies and SAST in one.
- **W5. Single runs, no statistics.** Most studies report one run of non-deterministic models without variance (§1). zhou2024's results rest on about 8–10 test CVEs per language [I] [@zhou2024comparison, p. 6]. xiong's real-world samples are 50 alerts each [@xiong2026sifting, p. 13]. shu chooses the best of ~30 configurations post hoc [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17].
- **W6. Little cost reporting.** Ten of 16 primary studies report no monetary cost (§1). Where cost is measured it is decisive: up to $1,247.66 per project [@li2026llm, p. 16].
- **W7. Narrow scope.** Data are C/C++-biased and long-tailed, and 555 mappable CWEs appear in no analysed dataset [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 34]. 87 studies build custom datasets and only nine datasets are reused in more than ten studies [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 35]. Only one of 40 detection studies to March 2024 worked at repository level [@zhou2025large, p. 18].
- **W8. Three-way comparisons are rare.** [I] Only khare evaluates LLMs, SAST and DL in one study, and its SAST arm covers synthetic data only [@khare2025understanding, p. 7]. zhou2024 compares fine-tuned and prompted LLMs with SAST but no classic DL detector [@zhou2024comparison, p. 4].
- **W9. Preprint text vs version of record.** Nine published papers were analysed from arXiv text, and du2026reducing from a v1 with a placeholder header [@du2026reducing, p. 2]. zhou2025large's only LLM-vs-SAST study is the authors' own zhou2024comparison [@zhou2025large, p. 22], so it is not independent support.
- **W10. Independence.** [I] guo and li2026llm share five C/C++ modules. ding, yildiz and tan share PrimeVul. Duplication figures reused elsewhere trace back to ding alone (critical review B).

## 6. What this means for our research questions

**RQ1 — effectiveness head-to-head.** No family wins across settings. Frontier LLMs beat SAST on small, self-contained code [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10; @dubniczky2025castle, p. 11]. CodeQL beats LLMs on synthetic function-level suites [@khare2025understanding, p. 9]. At project scale, general coding agents reach much higher recall than SAST (59.55% vs 0–34.29% on C/C++) [@li2026llm, p. 7], but most LLM detectors and SAST tools produce mostly false warnings [@li2026llm, p. 11]. Against fine-tuned DL, the ranking depends on dataset and class balance [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40], and all families are near or below chance on PrimeVul pairs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9; @tan2026think, p. 6]. **Strength: weak to moderate.** Results come from single-run studies with incompatible metrics and no pooling. The most robust pattern is "LLMs higher recall, lower precision" [I].

**RQ2 — evaluation setups.** Setup explains much of the disagreement. Sources of variation:
- label noise (39–65% correct) [@risse2025top, p. 8];
- leakage [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4];
- balanced vs realistic class ratios [@shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7];
- synthetic vs real code [@khare2025understanding, p. 5];
- function vs statement granularity [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8];
- custom datasets with inconsistent splits [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 35].

**Strength: moderate to strong**, consistent across independent primary studies and two SLRs.

**RQ3 — hybrids.** LLM filtering of SAST alarms removes most false alarms at cents per alarm but loses 12–25% of real bugs [@du2026reducing, p. 8; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18]; **moderate**. Hybrid detection (IRIS, RepoAudit) beats SAST in the authors' own evaluations [@li2024iris, p. 8; @guo2025repoaudit, p. 8] but not in an independent project-scale study [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 12]. The gain depends on a strong LLM [@li2024iris, p. 10]; **weak/contested**. Costs range from cents to $1,247.66 per project, against minutes and no token cost for SAST [@li2026llm, p. 16]. LLMs mislocate findings [@gnieciak2025large, p. 11] [A], and fluent explanations do not signal correctness [@tan2026think, p. 9], which limits explainability.

**RQ4 — CWEs, languages, scale.** LLMs do best on self-contained injection-style CWEs and worst on context-dependent, crypto/policy and memory-safety localisation [@khare2025understanding, p. 7; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18; @shu2026evaluating, p. 30]. CodeQL is better on CWE-190 [@khare2025understanding, p. 8]. LLM performance falls with function or file length [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 13; @li2026llm, p. 9]. Evidence is concentrated on C/C++ and Java [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 28]. **Strength: weak.** Per-CWE cells are small and per-CWE results diverge across studies; for example, khare finds LLMs beat CodeQL on CWE-476 [@khare2025understanding, p. 8], while ahmed reports over-flagging of it [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 13].

**RQ5 — open problems.** Recurring problems:
- verified, realistic, repository-level benchmarks with context [@zhou2025large, p. 19; @risse2025top, p. 12];
- same-benchmark three-way comparisons (W8);
- independent labelling and statistics (W3, W5);
- cost reporting (W6);
- contamination control (W2);
- true-positive loss in filtering [@xiong2026sifting, p. 19];
- workflow integration: none of 58 reviewed studies was integrated into developer workflows [@zhou2025large, p. 19].

**Strength: moderate** as a description of recurring limitations. [I] These are candidate gaps only until the novelty checks in `gap-report.md` are run (standards §7).

# Methodology comparison — LLM-based vs traditional static analysis and deep learning for source-code vulnerability detection

- Project: `2026-11-12-llm-based-vs-traditional-static-analysis`
- Date: 2026-11-12
- Inputs: 20 analyses (`status: complete`, all full text), `evidence-matrix.md`, `literature-matrix.md`, critical reviews A and B of 2026-11-12.
- Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data, **[A]** author claim, **[I]** our interpretation. Unlabelled numeric statements are [V] from the cited page.
- Source tiers: three items are recorded by `rlab` as arXiv preprints. IRIS [@li2024iris, p. 1] and RepoAudit [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 1] are the ICLR 2025 and ICML 2025 camera-ready texts. Only zhou2024comparison is a true preprint without a known peer-reviewed version (**not peer-reviewed**) [@zhou2024comparison, p. 1]. Nine further papers were read in their arXiv versions, not the version of record (see §5, W9).

A short glossary for readers new to the area: *SAST* (static application security testing) tools such as CodeQL or Semgrep scan code with hand-written rules. *DL detectors* (e.g. LineVul, Devign) are neural networks trained on labelled vulnerable code. A *balanced* test set has 50% vulnerable samples. *Pairwise correctness (P-C / pAcc)* is the share of vulnerable/patched function pairs where both versions are classified correctly. *SFDR* is the sampled false discovery rate, i.e. the share of a tool's warnings that are false.

## 1. Overview table

| Paper | Tier / text read | Design | Data, N, unit | Metrics | Comparators | Statistics / runs | Data & code |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ahmed2026secvuleval [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 6; @ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8] | AIware 2026; arXiv v1 | Benchmark + 5 LLMs in a multi-agent pipeline | SecVulEval 25,440 C/C++ functions; detection on 300 functions (~120 vulnerable) | P/R/F1 at function and statement level (manual judging) | none outside LLMs | one run; Mann-Whitney only for function length [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 13] | dataset + code public [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 3] |
| chakraborty2024revisiting [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 4] | TSE; arXiv author copy | Replication of 4 DL detectors + 2 fine-tuned LLMs on new realistic data | Real-Vul: 5,528 vulnerable + ~1.68M "uncertain" functions, 10 C/C++ projects, time split | Acc, P, R, F1, AUC | DeepWukong, LineVul, ReVeal, IVDetect; CodeLlama, Mixtral | no CIs; Mann-Whitney in side analyses only [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 10] | Zenodo [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 2] |
