  - code version: older commits vs current HEAD (the five overlapping modules are only in li's real-world set);
  - metric: precision vs recall/SFDR;
  - labeller: authors vs Codex;
  - scale: avg 251 KLoC vs multi-million-LOC modules.

  [I] RepoAudit depends on source/sink API coverage. li records zero-token runs and 108/108 misses from API modelling [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 16]. This is unresolved.
- **C3. LLM vs SAST.** LLMs beat SAST on 10 small C# projects [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10] and on CASTLE C micro-programs [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11]. CodeQL beats the best LLM in accuracy on OWASP, Juliet Java and Juliet C/C++ [@khare2025understanding, p. 9]. At repository level, LLMs detect more but mark up to 77.4% of functions [@zhou2024comparison, p. 7] (preprint). There, general agents have the highest recall, while specialised LLM detectors and SAST have near-zero recall on some CWEs and 75–100% SFDR [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11]. The studies differ in language, unit (project/program/function/repository), synthetic vs real code, and scoring: a location rule applied only to LLMs [@gnieciak2025large, p. 6], and a CASTLE prompt that reveals the scoring rule [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 9]. [I] Synthetic suites match SAST rules, and small programs fit in an LLM's context. Real repositories defeat both families, so there is no single winner.
- **C4. Does reasoning reduce false positives?** Supporting it: reasoning models "consistently produced fewer false positives" [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 14], and RepoAudit precision rises to 82.35–88.46% with reasoning backbones [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 16]. Against it:
  - DeepSeek R1 has 166 FP vs GPT-4o's 116 in CASTLE's own table [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11];
  - thinking mode raises F1 through recall with unchanged accuracy, and its benefit turns negative under dual- and multi-agent designs [@tan2026think, p. 6; @tan2026think, p. 8];
  - reasoning LLMs are near chance on REEF [@shu2026evaluating, p. 37].

  [I] The claim holds for OpenAI o-series models in some settings and does not generalise.
- **C5. Class balance flips the ranking.** On balanced REEF, fine-tuned GPT-4o + few-shot beats CodeT5P (Acc 0.7196 vs 0.6037) [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17]. On the imbalanced test, PLMs win (UniXcoder F1 0.4626 vs GPT-4o 0.4010) [@shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @shu2026evaluating, p. 41]. Likewise, yildiz's F1 falls from ~49–65% on balanced pairs to 5.41–12.21% on non-paired PrimeVul [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7]. [I] Balanced sets reward liberal flagging, so balanced-benchmark rankings do not transfer to deployment.
- **C6. Hybrid IRIS.** IRIS+GPT-4 beats CodeQL on 120 Java CVEs (55 vs 27; AvgFDR 84.82% vs 90.03%) [@li2024iris, p. 8]. Yet on real-world Java, IRIS has 97.80% SFDR vs 77.00% for CodeQL [@li2026llm, p. 12]. The comparison is not like-for-like: known CVEs vs new code, detections vs SFDR, and different labelling. [I] Hybrids may raise recall on benchmark CVEs while adding noise on unseen code. This is open.

(b) For evidence-matrix.md:

## Agreements / converging evidence

- **G1. Realistic evaluation collapses performance (strong).**
  - DL precision falls to 1–10% on Real-Vul [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 7].
  - Code-LM F1 falls from 62.88–68.26% to 18.05–21.43% within PrimeVul and 1.91–5.82% cross-dataset [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7].
  - LLM accuracy is 10.5% lower on real-world data than on synthetic data [@khare2025understanding, p. 5].
  - Line-level F1 falls from 0.6641 to 0.3450 on 2024–25 code [@shu2026evaluating, p. 39].
  - Statement-level scoring halves F1 [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8].

  Surveys concur [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 39; @sheng2025llms, p. 20].
- **G2. Benchmark labels are noisy (strong).** Two independent audits find 39–65% [@risse2025top, p. 8] and 24–36% [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4] of vulnerable labels correct, and ReVeal has 15% label inconsistency [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 3]. The 25% BigVul figure is Chen et al.'s via Ding and is not independent.
- **G3. Prompted LLMs over-flag and cannot separate vulnerable from patched code (moderate).**
  - GPT-4 two-shot calls both versions vulnerable in 71.63% of pairs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9].
  - "Both vulnerable" accounts for 40–95% of failures [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 8].
  - The dual-agent design flags 88.2% of functions [@tan2026think, p. 7].
  - Always-vulnerable rows appear among khare's best F1 values [@khare2025understanding, p. 16].

  These are partly one dataset family (PrimeVul).
- **G4. SAST recall is low on real code and high only on synthetic suites (moderate).**
  - Best single tools detect 30.0–44.4% of CVEs, and many detect 0% [@zhou2024comparison, p. 6].
  - CodeQL recall is 6.00–34.29% on C/C++ and 14.19% on Java [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 9].
  - CodeQL finds 27/120 on CWE-Bench-Java [@li2024iris, p. 8].
  - On CASTLE, CodeQL reaches 29% and the SAST average is 23% [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 12].
  - In contrast, CodeQL accuracy is 0.94 on Juliet Java [@khare2025understanding, p. 9].
- **G5. CodeQL on OWASP replicates across groups (moderate).** khare reports P 0.58 / R 0.96 / F1 0.72 [@khare2025understanding, p. 9]; xiong reports P 60.3% / R 97.0% / F1 74.4% [@xiong2026sifting, p. 11].
- **G6. Missing context is the shared failure cause (moderate).**
  - All 151 truly vulnerable audited functions need external context [@risse2025top, p. 9].
  - Context-type identification is ≤41.33% [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 9].
  - API modelling explains 108/108 RepoAudit (GPT-5.4) misses [@li2026llm, p. 7], and 14.60% of FPs come from truncated inter-procedural context [@li2026llm, p. 15].
- **G7. LLM filtering of SAST alarms trades large false-positive reduction for lost true positives (moderate).** du2026reducing removes 94–98% of false alarms with real-bug recall of 0.75–0.88 [@du2026reducing, p. 8]. xiong2026sifting reaches FPR 6.3% with a 22.25% miss rate [@xiong2026sifting, p. 12; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18]. du involves the authors' own method, Tencent-affiliated authors and non-security bug types.
- **G8. Prompt-only LLMs trail adapted models (moderate).**
  - Fine-tuned models beat prompted ChatGPT on Big-Vul [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4].
  - GPT-3.5 prompting detects 3.7–23.2% vs 89.2% for fine-tuned CodeBERT [@zhou2024comparison, p. 10].
  - Prompt-only LLMs are near chance on REEF [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17].
- **G9. LLM cost far exceeds SAST cost and varies by orders of magnitude (moderate).** SAST runs in minutes with no token cost, while RepoAudit averages $172.77 per project [@li2026llm, p. 16]. Alarm filtering costs under $0.20 per alarm [@du2026reducing, p. 8; @xiong2026sifting, p. 17]. GPT-4o instruction tuning costs about 15× a PLM run [@shu2026evaluating, p. 42].

(c) "Current answer" for RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md:

**RQ1:** No family wins across settings. Frontier LLMs beat SAST on small, self-contained code [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10; @dubniczky2025castle, p. 11], but CodeQL beats LLMs on synthetic function-level suites [@khare2025understanding, p. 9]. At project scale, general coding agents reach much higher recall than SAST (59.55% vs 0–34.29% on C/C++), while most LLM detectors and SAST tools produce mostly false warnings [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11]. Against fine-tuned DL, the ranking depends on dataset and class balance [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40], and all families are near or below chance on PrimeVul pairs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9; @tan2026think, p. 6]. Strength: weak to moderate (single-run studies, incompatible metrics, no pooling); the most robust pattern is "LLMs have higher recall and lower precision" [I].

**RQ2:** Evaluation setup explains much of the disagreement:
- label noise (39–65% correct) [@risse2025top, p. 8];
- exact-copy leakage up to 18.9% [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4];
- balanced vs realistic class ratios that flip rankings [@shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7];
- synthetic vs real code [@khare2025understanding, p. 5];
- function vs statement granularity [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8];
- custom datasets with inconsistent splits [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 35].

Strength: moderate to strong (consistent across independent primary studies and two SLRs).

**RQ3:** LLM filtering of SAST alarms removes most false alarms at under $0.20 per alarm but loses 12–25% of real bugs [@du2026reducing, p. 8; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18]; strength moderate. Hybrid detection (IRIS, RepoAudit) beats SAST in the authors' own evaluations [@li2024iris, p. 8; @guo2025repoaudit, p. 8] but not in an independent project-scale study [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 12], and the gain needs a strong LLM [@li2024iris, p. 10]; strength weak/contested. LLM costs range from cents per alarm to $1,247.66 per project, against minutes and no token cost for SAST [@li2026llm, p. 16]. Explainability is limited: LLMs mislocate findings [@gnieciak2025large, p. 11], and fluent explanations do not signal correctness [@tan2026think, p. 9].

**RQ4:** LLMs do best on self-contained injection-style CWEs. They do worst on context-dependent and crypto/policy CWEs and on localising memory-safety bugs [@khare2025understanding, p. 7; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18; @shu2026evaluating, p. 30]. CodeQL is better on CWE-190 [@khare2025understanding, p. 8]. LLM performance falls with function and file length [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 13; @li2026llm, p. 9], and evidence is concentrated on C/C++ and Java [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 28]. Strength: weak (small per-CWE cells; per-CWE results diverge across studies).

**RQ5:** Recurring open problems:
- verified, realistic, repository-level benchmarks with context [@zhou2025large, p. 19; @sheng2025llms, p. 25];
- same-benchmark comparisons of LLM vs SAST vs DL (only khare runs all three, with SAST on synthetic data only [@khare2025understanding, p. 7]);
- independent labelling and statistical testing [@li2026llm, p. 11];
- cost reporting;
- contamination control;
- true-positive loss in filtering [@xiong2026sifting, p. 19];
- workflow integration: none of the 58 studies reviewed by zhou2025large is integrated into developer workflows [@zhou2025large, p. 19].

Strength: moderate as a description of recurring limitations [I]. These are candidate gaps until the novelty checks in gap-report.md are done.
